DRAFT · Nov 26, 2026

Curvature-dial survey: which proved laws slide into one another

Turning the curvature dial d with k held fixed: three stops at k = 0, nothing in between, and finite clocks on the turning side at k ≠ 0.

Curvature-dial survey: which proved laws slide into one another (DRAFT)

DRAFT, Nov 26 2026. Part of Affine Composition Theory (repo: fused-hyperoperation-algebra). Asked for by Brennan: "I'd like similar surveys for the other dials as well", the same survey as the shape-dial one ("a survey of all of our laws that we've proven to see if the shape dial is able to move from one to another … really all of them", then "check all laws … to see if a new law emerges and what it might be for", with a cheap polishing step). This page does it for d, the curvature dial: the plane law a ∘ b = (a + b + k·ab)/(1 − d·ab), with k held fixed. Curvature = −Δ/4 with Δ = k² − 4d is a reading, never an input. Checks: checks.py → checks_output.txt, 65 of 65 pass (sympy exact, numpy/scipy numeric; 4 polish checks with mpmath at 30 digits cost 0.05 s; the whole script takes about 1 min 45 s, nearly all sympy). Law list: laws.py → laws.json. Pictures: figures.py → figures/. No Lean in this pass. Colour key: blue = our reading, orange = already known, grey = endpoints / background.

The result

I sorted the 65 law groups of dial-catalog/catalog.py. Holding k fixed and turning only d:

  • 17 groups slide into another proved law, with the carrying quantity checked along the whole dial.
  • 3 are plausible: the numbers slide, the law in between is not proved (rung heights, cube face weights, Newton's G).
  • 6 survive on part of the dial and break on the rest (Bayes, the union rule, Maxwell's wave equation, causal-diamond counting, π, Euler's identity).
  • 1 is another parameter in disguise (the elliptic modulus moves the t⁴ term, off the (k, d) plane).
  • 1 is the dial itself (the plane law).
  • 37 do not slide (they live on the k dial, the shape dial, or do not use d).

The plain conclusion. At k = 0 the d dial has exactly three stops and nothing in between: every d < 0 is Einstein's addition for some light speed, d = 0 is Galileo, every d > 0 is tangent addition with some scale (section N3, proved). Almost every slide in this survey is that one three-way switch read in a different field: two walls, one wall at infinity, no wall. At k ≠ 0 the switch moves to the parabola d = k²/4, and the turning side gains a ladder of special settings, the finite clocks (section N1). All of this is the Cayley–Klein / Yaglom family and Coleman–McGuinness's classification (1991); the survey's own part is which proved laws ride on it and the corner reading below.

The leads, in order, each judged on its own:

  1. Corner weights become Lucas numbers (C2), slides. The n-fold plane law is a ratio of two corner sums, and a corner of size n carries the Lucas number U_n(k, d) = αⁿ⁻¹[n]_q. At d = 0 this is the cube's corner expansion; at k = 0 it is the tangent-sum formula; in between it is q-counting. Worth following as an organising formula: it puts three proved modules (Base/Cube, q-counting, the genus) on one line. The pieces are classical; the corner reading was not found in my search.
  2. Finite clocks on the turning side (N1), proved, elementary. At d/k² = 1/(4cos²(πj/N)), "add infinity" has exact order N, the size-N corner weight vanishes, q is an N-th root of unity, and the χ_y parameter is minus a root of unity, which is Hirzebruch's level-N cusp value (1988). Each piece is known; the bundle is a tidy explainer, not a new theorem.
  3. Jets: finite difference → derivative → complex step (C11), slides. In R[u]/(u² − ku + d), f(a + bu) samples f at two points that merge on the parabola and go complex past it. Known pieces (Lyness and Moler 1967; Squire and Trapp 1998); the placement on the dial is ours. Useful as an explainer and for numerics, not a research lead.
  4. Physics slides that are all known and all consistent (C3, C4, C12, C13). The twist turns on with d (Thomas, Foucault); Kepler's velocity space has curvature −2E; the carrier mass is m² = −d; a barrier and a beam splitter are one twist B_d(u) at d = ∓1. Good checks of the theory, no new prediction.
  5. Negative results, useful. Nothing new lives between the k = 0 stops (N3). The elliptic modulus is a second road that meets the d road only at its ends (C15). Waves, light cones and probability need two walls; π and Euler's identity need none (C6, C7, C10).

Figure 0. A: at k = 0, turning d moves the walls ±1/√(−d) in from infinity (orange, Einstein side) or replaces them by a turn whose quarter is π/(2√d) (blue, tangent side). Galileo sits between. B: the (k, d) plane. The survey runs on the line k = 0 and then on k = 1. The parabola d = k²/4 is where the kind changes. Hirzebruch's χ_y line d = k − 1 passes the Todd genus (the circle operation ∘₁), the Euler characteristic (on the parabola) and the signature (Einstein at c = 1). Blue squares on k = 1: the finite clocks of section N1.

Figure 1. All 65 groups, sorted by verdict. The candidate number is in brackets.

How I tested a slide

For each group I read the Lean module and the topic page it rests on, held k fixed, and turned d. A group slides when both ends are proved (a Lean theorem or a checked page) and the quantity that carries one end into the other is checked along the whole dial: exactly (sympy) where a closed form exists, numerically elsewhere. Plausible means the numbers move but the law in between is not proved. Partly means the law holds on one side and fails on the other. Two facts are used everywhere:

  • Units (check A6, Lean Landscape.units_den). Rescaling a ↦ λa moves (k, d) to (λk, λ²d). So at k = 0 only the sign of d is a law; its size is a unit.
  • Charts (check A7). A chart x ↦ x/(1 + cx) that fixes 0 moves (k, d) to (k − 2c, d − kc + c²) and keeps Δ. So at fixed k, turning d is the same as turning Δ, up to a chart. With charts and units together only the sign of Δ survives: the three kinds of Coleman–McGuinness. With units alone, d/k² is an invariant, and that is what C2, C8, C9 and N1 read.

C1. Galileo ↔ Einstein ↔ tangent: walls come in from infinity — slides (and the dial itself)

Figure 2. A: a ⊕ 0.5 at k = 0 for five settings of d. Einstein's curves saturate at the walls ±1; Galileo's is a straight line; the tangent curves run off and wrap. B: at k = 1 the circle operation (d = 0) already has two walls; the far wall comes in from infinity as d leaves 0, and the two walls merge at d = 1/4.

  • Both ends proved. Galileo, Einstein and tangent addition are NumberPlane.dual_point, split_point, complex_point and GroupsLie.theta_dual, theta_velocity, theta_tan; associativity for every (k, d) is Landscape.assoc_num/den (check A2).
  • The carrying quantity. At k = 0 the law is T_d(T_d⁻¹a + T_d⁻¹b) with T_d(t) = tan(√d·t)/√d, one function that is entire in d: tanh for d < 0, the identity at d = 0, tan for d > 0 (A1, polished to 30 digits in Q1). Einstein at d = −1/c² gives 0.5c ⊕ 0.6c = 0.846c (A3).
  • Crossing d = 0. The walls ±1/√(−d) run off to infinity as d → 0⁻ (A4). Past zero there is no wall: the value runs to infinity at rapidity π/(2√d) and wraps round (A5). The flow x′ = 1 + dx² (BeyondOneLoop.plane_generator) is T_d(t), and its wall exponents ∓2√(−d) shrink to 0 at d = 0 (A8): the marginal "creep like 1/L" of the parabola.
  • At k ≠ 0. d = 0 is no longer special: it is the circle operation ∘ₖ, still two walls (A9). The kind changes at d = k²/4.
  • Known (orange): the Cayley–Klein family and its velocity laws (Yaglom 1979; Herranz, Ortega and Santander 2000; Lévy-Leblond 1976); Coleman and McGuinness (1991), also Bismuth (1976, unpublished thesis). Ours (blue): nothing new here; this is the frame the rest of the survey uses.
  • Verdict: solid, known. It is the dial's own picture.

C2. Corner weights become Lucas numbers — slides

Figure 3. The weight U_n(k, d) of an n-element corner, at k = 1. At d = 0 every weight is kⁿ⁻¹ = 1 (the cube). Turning d spreads them; each U_N first vanishes at a finite-clock setting (red dots, section N1).

  • The formula (B1, sympy, n = 2 to 5). x₁ ∘ … ∘ xₙ = Σ_S U_|S|(k, d)·x^S / (1 − d·Σ_S U_|S|−1(k, d)·x^S), sums over nonempty corners S, where U is the Lucas sequence U₀ = 0, U₁ = 1, U_{n+1} = k·U_n − d·U_{n−1}. Proof in one line: in the number plane u² = ku − d, ∏(1 + x_j u) = A + Bu with u^m = U_m u − d·U_{m−1}, and (1 + au)(1 + bu) = (1 − dab)(1 + (a ∘ b)u).
  • Both ends. At d = 0, U_n = kⁿ⁻¹ and the formula is the cube's corner expansion 1 + k(x₁ ∘ … ∘ xₙ) = ∏(1 + kx_j) (B2; Lean Base, Cube). At k = 0 the odd corners go to the numerator and the even ones to the denominator: (e₁ − d e₃)/(1 − d e₂ + d² e₄), the tangent-sum formula (B3).
  • Powers and the lift. The lift 1 + kx becomes the norm V(x) = 1 + kx + dx², which multiplies up to the square of the denominator: V(a ∘ b)(1 − dab)² = V(a)V(b) (B4, Lean NumberPlane.norm_mul). So 1 + k a⁽ⁿ⁾ = (1 + ka)ⁿ becomes V(a⁽ⁿ⁾)·(den)² = V(a)ⁿ (B5).
  • q-counting is the same weight. U_n = αⁿ⁻¹·[n]_q with α + β = k, αβ = d, q = β/α (B6). So the corner weight is a q-integer, and d sets q.
  • Known: Lucas sequences (Lucas 1878) and their Binet form; the tangent-sum formula with elementary symmetric functions; the norm of a quadratic algebra. Ours: the n-fold plane law as a corner sum with Lucas weights, which ties the cube's corner expansion, the tangent sum and [n]_q together. Not found in my search (queries listed under Known vs new).
  • Verdict: worth following as an organising formula. It is short, exact for every (k, d), and joins three proved modules. It is not a deep theorem.

C3. The twist turns on with d — slides

Figure 4. The twist ω for two fixed half-velocities as d is turned. Zero at d = 0, opposite signs on the two sides.

  • The law (Lean TwistedBoosts.twist_half_angle): tan(ω/2) = d(u × v)/(1 − d u·v). At d = 0 there is no twist in any directions (galilean_no_twist, check C2). The sign of the twist follows the sign of d (C3).
  • The carrying quantity, checked independently (C1). |ω| equals |d| × the area of the triangle (0, u, u ⊕ v), with the area from L'Huilier's formula on the sphere (d > 0) and the hyperbolic plane (d < 0): 80 random pairs, error 3e-15.
  • What rides on it (from gravity-from-theory/spinning-river/ figure 5, which sorted 17 frame ideas by dial): d = +1, Foucault, Coriolis, Larmor and Berry; d = 0, Galilean boosts and river cells, nothing precesses; d = −1, Thomas–Wigner, geodetic, Lense–Thirring (checked against Gravity Probe B and the double pulsar in twisted-boosts/).
  • Known: Thomas (1926), Wigner (1939), Ungar's gyrogroups, Gauss–Bonnet. Ours (repo): the twist as the phase of the split corner, read off the curvature dial.
  • Verdict: solid, known. A clean picture of the d dial switching precession on.

C4. Number planes, Clifford's ω², and Kepler's velocity space — slides

Figure 5. A: the unit "circle" x² + dy² = 1 is a circle, two parallel lines (d = 0) or a hyperbola. B: Kepler hodographs (velocity curves). Bound orbits close, the parabolic one passes through v = 0, the escaping one stays outside the dotted circle |v| = v∞.

  • Number planes (D1, D2; Lean NumberPlane, Clifford.division_cases). In R[u]/(u² + d), slopes compose by (s₁ + s₂)/(1 − d s₁s₂). The norm x² + dy² splits into two light-cone factors (d < 0), is one square (d = 0) or never vanishes (d > 0). Clifford's biquaternion unit ω² = +1, 0, −1 (1873) is d = −1, 0, +1, one generator at a time.
  • Kepler (D3–D5). Hodographs are circles with |centre|² − R² = 2E (E = −0.2, 0, 0.3, error under 1e-6). Fock's velocity metric 2|dv|/(|v|² − 2E) has curvature exactly −2E (sympy). So the energy is the curvature dial: bound orbits on the turning side, the parabola at the flat stop, escape on the two-wall side. On the escape side the wall is the circle |v| = v∞ = √(2E): every speed stays above it (D4), as every velocity stays below c in relativity. The repo's κ = −1/(2E) (gravity-from-theory/ N9) is the κ-stereographic chart's parameter; it has the same sign, and the size is a unit choice (A6).
  • Known: complex, dual and double numbers (Yaglom 1979); Clifford (1873); Hamilton's hodograph (1846), Fock (1935), Moser (1970), Milnor (1983). Ours: reading the escape speed v∞ as the wall of the d < 0 chart (a small reading).
  • Verdict: solid, known. Kepler is the clearest physical case of all three stops on one dial.

C5. Pinched cubics: split node → cusp → non-split node — slides

Figure 6. Smooth points of y² + xy = x³ + a₂x² over F₁₃ for every a₂. The count is p − 1, p or p + 1 as the d dial moves the curve between the three kinds.

  • The pinched cubic y² + a₁xy = x³ + a₂x² sits at (k, d) = (−a₁, −a₂) (Lean Elliptic.node_param, walls_are_branches). Over F_p it has p − 1 smooth points (split node, two walls), p (cusp, the parabola) or p + 1 (non-split node, turning), as Δ = a₁² + 4a₂ is a nonzero square, zero or a non-square (E1, all d for p = 7, 11, 13).
  • Known: the group of smooth points of a singular cubic is the multiplicative group, the additive group, or a norm-one torus (Silverman, The Arithmetic of Elliptic Curves, §III.2). Ours (repo): the placement on the dial, already drawn in elliptic/.
  • Verdict: solid, known. Only the pinched curves ride the dial; smooth elliptic curves are off the plane (C15).

C6. Anchors: Möbius kinds, and why probability needs two walls — slides (Lie groups), partly (Bayes, union rule)

Figure 7. At k = −1, the two fixed points (anchors) of every move x ↦ x ∘ c. At d = 0 they are 1 (certainty) and infinity. They merge at d = 1/4 and then vanish.

  • The Lie-group slide (Lean GroupsLie.mob_dial, theta_*). The plane law is a Möbius product; turning d carries a hyperbolic one-parameter group (two fixed points) into a parabolic one (one) and an elliptic one (none). The fixed points are the roots of 1 + kx + dx² (F1; rulecraft-history/ H15).
  • Bayes and the union rule survive only while Δ > 0. At k = −1 every d < 1/4 is the union rule x + y − xy in a moved chart plus units (F2): "certainty" is just the moved anchor. No chart reaches d ≥ 1/4, because charts keep Δ and union has Δ = 1 > 0 (F3). Bayes in odds form is the same story at k = 1. Past the parabola there is no bounded slider to keep (rulecraft-history §7: "Δ < 0 rules have no anchor").
  • Known: Möbius maps sorted by the discriminant and commuting exactly when they share fixed points (textbook). Ours (repo): Δ as the anchor count, and what it means for odds and rules.
  • Verdict: solid, known. A clear "partly": probability lives on one side of the parabola.

C7. Waves and light cones need walls — partly (Maxwell, causal-diamond counting)

Figure 8. The d-boost keeps the operator ∂ₓ² + d∂ₜ². For d < 0 its characteristics form a light cone; as d → 0⁻ the cone opens flat; for d > 0 there is no cone, only ellipses (Laplace).

  • The law (G1, sympy): ∂ₓ² + d∂ₜ² is unchanged by the d-boost t′ = γ(t + dvx), x′ = γ(x − vt), γ = (1 + dv²)^(−1/2), and two d-boosts compose by (v + w)/(1 − dvw) (G2). So each d has its own invariant operator: a wave equation with c² = −1/d for d < 0, a degenerate ∂ₓ² at d = 0, Laplace's operator for d > 0 (G3).
  • Maxwell (electromagnetism/): the wave equation survives a dial boost only at d = −1/c², and ε₀μ₀ fixes that d. On the whole d < 0 side Maxwell survives with its own c. At d = 0 it splits into the two Galilean limits of Le Bellac and Lévy-Leblond (1973). For d > 0 it is the Euclidean (Wick-rotated) theory with no propagation.
  • Causal-diamond counting (curved-space/): it needs a light cone. Every d < 0 gives the same counting (only units change); at d = 0 the cone opens flat and every pair is time-ordered; past it there is no order to count.
  • Known: all of it (Le Bellac and Lévy-Leblond 1973; Wick rotation; Myrheim 1978 and Meyer 1988 for counting). Verdict: not a lead. It says plainly where these laws live: on the two-wall side only.

C8. At fixed k, d reads as a height — plausible (rungs, Newton's G)

Figure 9. At k = 1, the rung height s = k²/Δ that matches the plane law's formal invariant. s = 1 at the circle operation, s → ∞ at the parabola, and negative (a rewind) on the turning side.

  • The quantity (H1, sympy). The exponential map of the plane law has iterative residue 1/3 − 4d/(3k²) = Δ/(3k²). Height s of e^x − 1 has residue 1/(3s) (height-flow/). So at fixed k, d sets a matching height s = k²/Δ (Lean Landscape.rung_equivalent): s = 1 at d = 0, s = 2 at d = k²/8, s → 0 as d → −∞ (H2).
  • Past the parabola, s is negative. At d = k²/2, s = −1: the turning law has the residue −1/3 of log(1 + x), the rewind of e^x − 1 (H3).
  • Why only plausible. The residue is a formal invariant (Écalle). It does not decide analytic conjugacy; the repo's horn size (closed-leads-revisit/) shows rungs carry more. And at k = 0 the conic laws' fingerprint is stuck at 3/10 for every d (H4), so d moves nothing formal there. Newton's G (newton-g/): the second-loop number 1/3 − 4d/(3k²) can be put anywhere by d, so gravity's 3/5 is a choice (d = −k²/5), as that page already concluded.
  • Known: iterative residues and their behaviour under iteration (Écalle). Ours (repo): the residue formula along the dial. Verdict: a tidy reading, not a lead.

C9. One genus, d picks the parameter — slides (Bell/Catalan, q-counting, toric), plausible (cube face weights)

Figure 10. At k = 1, the χ_y parameter y of each d (up to units). A: real y from the signature end (d → −∞) through Todd (d = 0) to Euler (the parabola). B: past the parabola y lies on the unit circle; the orange squares are minus the roots of unity, where the finite clocks of section N1 sit.

  • The reading (I1, I2). Each (k, d) with 1 + kx + dx² = (1 + αx)(1 + βx) is Hirzebruch's two-parameter genus. Up to units it is the χ_y genus at (1 − y, −y) (Lean Landscape.chi_y_line, chi_y_touch), with k²/d = −(1 − y)²/y. At fixed k, turning d runs the whole real χ_y family once: signature (y → 1) as d → −∞, Todd (y = 0) at d = 0, the Euler characteristic (y = −1) on the parabola. Past the parabola y = e^(iθ) is on the unit circle, with k²/d = 4 sin²(θ/2). So at fixed k the d dial does move along the χ_y family, once the units are taken out; in raw coordinates the χ_y line d = k − 1 is crossed only once.
  • The shape picks the polynomial (I3). h-vectors at q = −y: simplex [n]_q, cube (1 + q)ⁿ, permutohedron Eulerian, associahedron Narayana. All equal 1 at d = 0 (q = 0) and count corners on the parabola (q = 1): 4, 8, 24, 14, as in the shape-dial survey's C5. Cube face weights q^area ride the same q, but the law between is not proved.
  • Known: Hirzebruch (1966); toric h-vectors (Danilov, Stanley). Ours: "at fixed k, d is the χ_y parameter, and the turning side is |y| = 1". Likely folklore; treat it as a clean statement.
  • Verdict: tidy, mostly known. It is what makes the finite clocks of N1 meet Hirzebruch's level-N genera.

C10. π and i live only on the turning side — partly

Figure 11. The length of the ruler ∫dx/(1 + dx²) is π/√d for d > 0. For d ≤ 0 it never closes.

  • exp(πu/√d) = −1 at d = 0.37 in R[u]/(u² + d) (J1); at d = 0, exp(θu) = 1 + θu never returns; at d < 0 the real part is cosh θ ≥ 1. The ruler length is π/√d for d > 0 and diverges for d ≤ 0 (J2).
  • Known: all of it. Verdict: a clean "partly". Euler's identity is the turning side's statement, not the dial's.

C11. Jets: finite difference → derivative → complex step — slides

Figure 12. In R[u]/(u² − ku + d), f(a + bu) samples f at a + αb and a + βb, the roots of u² − ku + d. At k = 1 the two points are real (finite difference), merge on the parabola (a jet, dual numbers) and become a complex pair (complex step).

  • The law (K1, sympy). The u-part of f(a + bu) is the divided difference (f(a + αb) − f(a + βb))/(α − β). On the parabola it is b·f′(a + kb/2), the jet (K2). Checked for f = exp by matrix exponentials on both sides (K3). At k = 0, d = h², it is the complex-step derivative Im f(a + ih)/h, exact to 1e-12 at h = 1e-8 with no cancellation (K4).
  • Both ends proved. d = 0 is the jet-fields page's R[e]/(e² − ke), "two sample points k apart" (Lean JetFields); the parabola is the dual numbers (GroupsLie.theta_dual). The jet river (Schwarzschild, Kerr) sits at the flat middle (spinning-river/, Lean shear_sq) and does not slide.
  • Known: Hermite interpolation / the Chinese remainder theorem for R[u]/((u − α)(u − β)); dual numbers in automatic differentiation; the complex step (Lyness and Moler 1967; Squire and Trapp 1998). Ours: the three methods as three stops of one dial. No source in my search put them on one parameter.
  • Verdict: a useful explainer. It is practical (the complex step avoids cancellation) but not a research lead.

C12. Force reach: Yukawa → Coulomb → oscillating — slides

Figure 13. One-dimensional fields of −w″ − dw = δ. Yukawa for d < 0, Coulomb's −|x|/2 at d = 0, an oscillating field for d > 0.

  • What the repo proved (Lean ForceReach): drift_removal (the carrier mass is m² = Δ/4), double_root_iff_border (massless exactly on the parabola), raychaudhuri_is_law, yukawa_deff. At k = 0, m² = −d (L4 re-derives it).
  • The slide (L1–L3). exp(−√(−d)·r)/(4πr) solves ∇²φ + dφ = 0 off the source for every d (sympy): Yukawa with reach 1/√(−d) for d < 0, Coulomb at d = 0, an outgoing wave for d > 0. In one dimension the three Green's functions are checked, and both sides meet Coulomb's −|x|/2 at d = 0, the gap closing like √|d|.
  • What the repo reads on the turning side. force-reach/ reads Δ < 0 as a closed ruler, a circle of length 2π/√(−Δ) with a Kaluza–Klein tower of masses n√(−Δ). The open-space oscillating field above is the other reading of the same sign; neither is a short-range force.
  • Known: Yukawa (1935), Helmholtz's equation, Kaluza–Klein. Verdict: solid, known. A good consistency check: the massless forces sit exactly on the parabola.

C13. Tunnelling: one twist for barrier, free flight and beam splitter — slides

Figure 14. Amplitudes compose by the d dial; averaged over the phase, probabilities compose by ∘ₖ with k = −2d.

  • Both ends exact (M2, sympy). An SU(1,1) barrier [[a, b], [b̄, ā]] is diag(a, ā)·B₋₁(b/a), and an SU(2) beam splitter [[a, b], [−b̄, ā]] is diag(a, ā)·B₊₁(b/a), with B_d(u) = [[1, u], [−dū, 1]] the boost of twisted-boosts/.
  • The carrying quantity (M1). Averaged over the angle, half-chords t = (1 − cos√K·D)/(2K) compose by ∘ₖ with k = −2K, checked at K = −1, −0.3, 0.5, 1 (Lean Tunnelling.mean_law_curvature). Barrier odds ∘₂ at K = −1, plain addition at K = 0, the piling-up lemma ∘₋₂ at K = +1.
  • Known: SU(1,1) multilayers (Monzón, Sánchez-Soto and coauthors); Anderson, Thouless, Abrahams and Fisher (1980); Matsui (1993). Ours (repo): k = −2K, and the barrier as B₋₁. Verdict: solid. It is the clearest place where the d dial turns into the k dial (by averaging).

C14. Riemann pairs: the heat flow is the d dial — slides (as a reading)

Figure 15. Zeros of z² − sz + (p − 2t). Forward, the pair spreads on the line; rewound, it meets at t = −Δ/8 and turns into a complex pair.

  • z² − sz + (P − 2t) solves f_t = −f_zz: the sum (k) is kept and the product (d) slides by −2t (N1, Lean RiemannRound3.heat_pair_disc). Its discriminant is Δ + 8t, so the collision is the parabola (N2).
  • Known: de Bruijn (1950), Newman (1976), Rodgers and Tao (2020, Λ ≥ 0). Verdict: a clean reading, not a lead, as riemann/round3/ already found: the hypothesis needs a sign, and the dial gives none.

C15. The elliptic modulus is a second road — disguise

Figure 16. Laws with log′ = 1/√(1 + 2κt² + εt⁴). The d road (conic laws, ε = κ², through Galileo) and the modulus road (ε = 1, κ = 1 − 2m) meet only at κ = ±1.

  • At k = 0 the conic laws have log′ = 1/(1 + dt²) = 1/√(1 + 2dt² + d²t⁴): ε = κ² (O1). The modulus road keeps ε = 1 (O2). They meet at tan (m = 0, small swings) and tanh (m = 1, the separatrix) and nowhere else. The pendulum's κ = cos θ₀ (O3) and its quarter period K(m) ~ ln(4/√(1 − m)) at the separatrix (Q3, 30 digits) belong to the modulus, not to d.
  • Verdict: not a d-dial slide. The modulus moves the t⁴ term, off the (k, d) plane. The two roads share their ends, which is why elliptic-modulus/ calls it "a road round the border instead of through it".

N. New laws at in-between settings

At k = 0 there are none (N3). At k ≠ 0 the turning side has one family of special settings (N1), with one formal reading attached (N2).

N1. Finite clocks at d/k² = 1/(4cos²(πj/N)) — proved (elementary)

Figure 17. A: at the clock settings, repeating "add infinity" returns to 0 after N steps. B: where the settings sit on the turning side. The j = 1 settings are k²/d = 4cos²(π/N), the Beraha numbers; they crowd toward the parabola.

Statement. Fix k ≠ 0 and d > k²/4. Let α, β be the roots of x² − kx + d and q = β/α. The following are the same:

  1. d/k² = 1/(4cos²(πj/N)) with gcd(j, N) = 1;
  2. q is a primitive N-th root of unity;
  3. the move x ↦ x ∘ ∞ = −(1 + kx)/(dx) has exact order N;
  4. U_N(k, d) = 0 and U_n(k, d) ≠ 0 for 0 < n < N: corners of size N drop out of the numerator of C2;
  5. the χ_y parameter of (k, d) is y = −q, minus a primitive N-th root of unity.

Proof. k²/d = (α + β)²/(αβ) = q + 2 + 1/q = 4cos²(φ/2) for q = e^(iφ), so 1 ⇔ 2. The move in 3 has matrix [[−k, −1], [d, 0]], whose eigenvalues are −α and −β; its N-th power is scalar exactly when (α/β)^N = 1, so 2 ⇔ 3. Binet's form U_n = (αⁿ − βⁿ)/(α − β) gives 2 ⇔ 4. The relation k²/d = −(1 − y)²/y of C9 with y = −q gives 5. ∎ Checked: P1–P4 for N = 3 to 12 and every j (exact for N = 3, 4, 6: d = k², k²/2, k²/3), polished at N = 7 to 30 digits (Q4); P5 finds nothing like it on the two-wall side.

What it might be for. - A clock inside a turning law. At these settings the turning law contains Z/N through ∞. The repo's finite clocks (GroupsLie.f5_cyclic, f7_cyclic) were over finite fields; these are the real-number versions. - Truncated corner expansions. At a clock setting the size-N corners vanish from the numerator, so the n-fold law is shorter than it looks. - Hirzebruch's level-N genera. At the cusps of Γ₁(N), Hirzebruch's elliptic genus of level N reduces to χ_y with −y an N-th root of unity (Hirzebruch 1988). Condition 5 says these d are exactly those cusp values, read on the d dial. - Beraha numbers. At j = 1, k²/d = 4cos²(π/N), the Beraha numbers of Potts and chromatic-polynomial theory. The diamond-lattice page tested them and found no clustering in its map, so I claim no link beyond the shared numbers.

Known vs ours. Each equivalence is textbook: degenerate Lucas sequences (U_n = 0 exactly when α/β is a root of unity), finite-order elliptic Möbius maps (trace²/det = 4cos²(πj/N); Beardon 1983), and Hirzebruch's cusp values (1988). Ours: bundling them as the special in-between settings of the d dial. Verdict: a clean explainer, modest lead. It joins three repo modules (finite clocks, Lucas corners, the genus line), but I see no new theorem behind it.

N2. The clocks sit at negative rung heights — checked (formal), meaning a conjecture

The height reading of C8 puts the clocks at s = k²/Δ = −cot²(πj/N) (P6): s = −1/3 at N = 3, −1 at N = 4, −3 at N = 6. So the order-4 clock is exactly the setting with the residue of log(1 + x), the rewind of e^x − 1 (H3). This is a formal match only. I do not know whether it means anything; it is listed so nobody has to find it again.

N3. Nothing in between at k = 0 — proved

By units (A6, Lean Landscape.units_den), every d < 0 is Einstein's law with c = 1/√(−d) and every d > 0 is tangent addition with a scale. So the k = 0 line holds exactly three laws. Any law "between Galileo and Einstein" on one line must move k too, or leave the plane (as the modulus does, C15). Negative, and it saves effort.

Assumptions

  • Fixed k. Every verdict holds k fixed and turns d alone. Moves that change k and d together (the diamond lattice's Potts Q on k + d = −1, the χ_y line) are sorted as "no" or read through units.
  • Charts and units. "Same law" means equal after a linear rescaling (units). Where a Möbius chart is also allowed I say so (C6, A7). With both, only the sign of Δ survives.
  • Real numbers. The survey works over ℝ, except C5 (finite fields) and the complex readings of C9 and N1.
  • Numeric only: the twist-area check C1 (80 random pairs), Kepler D3–D4 (integrated orbits), the jets check K3–K4, the 1D Green's functions L2–L3, the averaged-chord check M1, and the clock orders P1–P3, P5 (floating point; N = 3, 4, 6 are exact, N = 7 is polished to 30 digits).
  • Formal only: C8 and N2 compare iterative residues, a formal invariant; they say nothing about analytic conjugacy.
  • Verdicts rest on the repo's own status of each Lean module and page; this pass re-checks only the quantities listed.
